name: Covariance Stabilization and Correction
text:
# Covariance Stabilization and Correction
## Overview
This family modifies the 2D screen-space covariance matrix of a Gaussian primitive to ensure numerical stability or correct projection errors before [rasterization](#15310-rasterization.md) [S1]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly adjusting covariance entries via low-pass filtering with density preservation or linear regression, rather than relying on geometric bounding heuristics [S1].
## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the 2D screen-space covariance matrix $\Sigma^{2D}$ derived from a 3D Gaussian [G]. The core mechanism involves modifying the matrix entries to ensure numerical stability (positive definiteness) or to correct for projection errors [S1]. The output is typically a corrected covariance matrix or its inverse (conic matrix) used in the rasterization kernel [G]. The methods assume the input covariance is symmetric and positive semi-definite [G].
## Subtopics

### [2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling](3467-2d-gaussian-covariance-stabilization-and-rescaling.md)
This method stabilizes the projection by applying a low-pass filter to the 2D covariance matrix, ensuring each Gaussian spans at least the width of a single pixel to reduce aliasing [3467-2d-gaussian-covariance-stabilization-and-rescaling]. It computes a rescale factor to preserve the integrated density of the Gaussian after filtering. Choose this when aliasing is a primary concern and density preservation is required. See [2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling](3467-2d-gaussian-covariance-stabilization-and-rescaling.md).

### [2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression](9912-2d-covariance-correction-via-linear-regression.md)
This method approximates the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances using a linear regression model, serving as a computationally efficient alternative to neural network-based corrections [9912-2d-covariance-correction-via-linear-regression]. It sets itself apart by replacing complex learned mappings with closed-form linear coefficients or a single scalar factor, reducing training overhead. Choose this when reconstruction quality comparable to Half-Cosine kernels is needed with lower computational cost. See [2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression](9912-2d-covariance-correction-via-linear-regression.md).

### Covariance Correction Factor
#### definition
A scalar correction factor applied to the covariance matrix to approximate the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances, replacing a more complex MLP or [Simpson's rule integration](#23099-simpson-s-rule-integration.md) [S1].
#### parameter
[Inverse Multiquadric](#9910-inverse-multiquadric-splatting.md) correction factor: 1.38f [S1].
Parabolic correction factor: 1.3f [S1].

## Background
The techniques originate from work on generalizing [splatting](#23-splatting.md) with decaying anisotropic radial basis functions [S1]. The correction methods were introduced to approximate the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances, replacing complex MLPs or Simpson's rule integration with linear regression or scalar factors [S1]. The stabilization approach addresses aliasing in novel view synthesis, while correction methods address the geometric mismatch between the projected Gaussian and the true integrated density [S1].
## Sources
[S1] DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00438, fetched 2026-10-30
